after: ## Step 1: from aim to research questions
alt: The aim of exploring how two football commentators construct excitement splits into three research questions: grammar at moments of high action, prosodic features such as pace, pitch and volume, and the effect of the radio or television context. A note contrasts this with a yes-or-no hypothesis.
caption: An aim says what you want to find out; each research question points to specific features and data.

alt: Two data sets are matched on length, context and date, and differ only in the factor being studied. If other variables also differ, a difference in the data cannot be put down to that factor.
caption: Hold everything else similar so any difference comes from the factor you are studying.

alt: Left: ethical steps of informed consent, anonymising speakers as labels such as Speaker A, storing data responsibly, and discussing any covert recording with a teacher. Right: Labov's observer's paradox, where recording people to capture unobserved talk may make their speech more careful or formal. Strategies below are longer recordings, familiar settings and an absorbing activity.
caption: Get consent, anonymise, and reduce the observer's paradox where you can; acknowledge what remains.

alt: The lesson's descriptive sentence about recording a family dinner is set above its evaluative version, which is split into three labelled parts: why the setting was chosen, the weakness of a single meal, and the improvement of a second recording.
caption: An evaluative methodology explains why, names the weakness and suggests an improvement.

alt: Analysis organised text by text slides into description, while analysis organised by research question compares all the data at once. Each section then runs through five steps: evidence, interpretation with terminology, testing theory against the data, contextual influences, and counter-examples.
caption: Organise by research question or feature, then give each section the same five moves.

alt: Four steps for the conclusion: answer each research question, state what the data suggests, qualify by sample size and context, and identify further research. Cautious wording such as "suggests", "in this data" and "may" is contrasted with the over-generalisation "all men interrupt".
caption: Answer each question, then qualify the claim by sample size and context.

alt: AO1 rewards methods of language analysis with terminology and coherent expression, AO2 critical understanding of concepts and issues, and AO3 analysis of how contextual factors and language features construct meaning. A thread of context runs through every section of the analysis.
caption: Contextual analysis (AO3) belongs in every section, not in a single paragraph.
